analysis.one_liner: Extends federal labor rights — overtime pay, sick leave, written contracts, breaks, and anti-discrimination protections — to the nation's 2.2 million domestic workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 9, 2025, with 17 Democratic and independent cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring the roughly 2.2 million people who clean homes, care for children, and serve as home health and personal care aides under basic federal workplace protections. It would end the current exemption that denies live-in domestic workers overtime pay, require written work agreements, guarantee paid sick time, meal and rest breaks, advance notice of schedule changes, and protections against retaliation. It would also extend workplace anti-discrimination protections to domestic workers and fund enforcement through a hotline, a standards board, and federal grants. As of now it has only been introduced and referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health and personal care aides, mostly women of color and immigrants earning a median of roughly $16.58 an hour — would gain overtime pay for live-in work, guaranteed paid sick time, written contracts, meal and rest breaks, protection from wage deductions and retaliation, and, for the first time, full anti-discrimination protections. Families and seniors who rely on home care would also benefit from lower turnover and steadier care.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act provision that has excluded live-in domestic workers from overtime pay, so live-in nannies, home care aides, and housekeepers would earn time-and-a-half beyond 40 hours a week.
Requires written, plain-language employment agreements covering pay, hours, duties, and termination policies, and bans forced arbitration clauses, noncompetes, and NDAs in those agreements.
Guarantees earned paid sick time — 1 hour per 30 worked, up to 56 hours a year — usable for the worker's own illness, caring for family, or domestic violence situations.
Guarantees meal and rest breaks, 72-hour advance notice of schedule changes with reporting-time pay, and the right to request temporary schedule changes for personal events.
Extends Title VII civil rights anti-discrimination protections to domestic workers, who are currently largely de facto excluded because of small-employer thresholds and misclassification.

Creates a Domestic Employee Standards Board, a national hotline, and grants for community-based education and enforcement, and gives the Labor Department investigative and subpoena authority to enforce the new rights.

analysis.who_pays: Household employers — including ordinary families who hire nannies and aides — would face new paperwork, scheduling, and overtime costs. Home care agencies and Medicaid-funded programs would absorb higher labor costs, partly offset by a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid match written into the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Household employers and home care agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes federal paperwork and labor standards on household employers, including ordinary families who hire nannies or home health aides — requiring written agreements, 72-hour schedule-change notice, and meal/rest break compliance — which could be burdensome for small, informal arrangements.

Overtime pay for live-in domestic workers and mandated severance or 30 days of lodging after termination raise costs for families relying on live-in care, and those costs may be passed on or reduce hiring.
A temporary federal Medicaid match (Title IV) would partially subsidize the higher labor costs for Medicaid-funded home care, meaning taxpayers share some of the bill's cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to an unusually vulnerable workforce — mostly women of color and immigrants earning around $16.58 an hour, facing wage theft and illegal deductions — are large and well documented in the bill's own findings. The main cost falls on household employers, who face real administrative burdens and, for live-in workers, potential termination and lodging obligations; for Medicaid-funded care, some cost shifts to public programs. The bill does little to mitigate the compliance burden on ordinary families hiring occasional help above the 8-hour threshold, which is its strongest good-faith criticism. Still, the core rights — sick leave, breaks, written terms, and an end to live-in overtime exclusion — address well-documented harms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which so far has taken no action on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 9, 2025 and read twice.
It was referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no markup or vote has occurred.
It has 17 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one independent, and no Republican support in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet; for now the bill sits in committee, so the status quo — domestic workers without federal labor protections — continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 Democratic colleagues to cosponsor it.

for.name: 17 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 16 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Booker, Fetterman, Duckworth, and Sen. King (I).

for.name: National Domestic Workers Alliance
for.what_they_did: Long championed a federal domestic workers bill of rights and its research is cited extensively in the bill's findings.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican has signed on, and the bill's fate rests with a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats.

industries.industry: Medicaid-funded home care agencies and fiscal intermediaries
industries.note: The bill requires labor standards for workers providing Medicaid-funded home and community-based services while encouraging use of fiscal intermediaries and temporarily raising the federal Medicaid match to fund compliance. Home care is overwhelmingly publicly financed, so the bill formalizes and stabilizes that publicly funded channel.
Platforms could no longer penalize workers for communicating directly with clients instead of through the platform's messaging system. This limits platforms' control over their workforce.

Families and agencies that employ nannies, aides, and housekeepers would face federal wage, scheduling, and contract obligations. Consumers of care could face higher prices, though better pay and conditions also improve care quality and reduce turnover.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and referral to the Senate HELP Committee with no markup scheduled, the bill is likely to sit without action, as similar domestic worker bills have in past Congresses. Its realistic path would be as part of a larger labor or care-economy package if the political balance shifts.
